items.title: Toshiko Akiyoshi interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 17, 1999
items.q: Even for example the greatest classic Miles Davis Quintet, like Red Garland, Philly Jo, Coltrane, Paul Chambers.

ctx.x: No. Actually I never thought about it until Duke Ellington died. Before that, you know it was just a Japanese traditional concept, or being Japanese playing jazz was some sort of a handicap. When I was growing up in Japan as a player, they always said that Filipino people have better feeling than Japanese, and indeed the Filipino players played better than us, and it’s simply because they have a longer history. They weren’t under — they were colonized by America so they are more exposed for jazz, much longer than…

So that has been going on for a long time. When Duke Ellington died, it was ’73, or ’74 I think, and there was a Village Voice, Nat Hentoff had a memoir. And he was talking about that fact that Duke was, how proud he was about his race. And he was pointing out so many music was based on his race, which I knew some…

However people always say that, you know I barely played for about thirteen years, and the people always say well you had a terrible time, a difficult time. And I never thought I am having a difficult time. Because everybody else did I thought. When I look back I think those times were very important times. items.q: Coltrane would get off the stage and go backstage and try and woodshed

ctx.x: Do you remember some of the groups that you were on the bill with? The other groups?

Oh yes. Sometimes it was Miles‟ group—only it was, John Coltrane was there after Sonny Rollins. That … the old Birdland‟s band room, backstage, it was like what we call … Japanese have a saying, “a bed for an eel.” In other words, long and narrow. And that‟s where the backstage was. But when it was Miles‟ group, they all played very long solos, except Miles didn‟t play long solos. But … he‟d [Coltrane] play a long solo, then it was … Coltrane would get off the stage and go backstage and try and woodshed. And so…

on the extreme right is the bar. That‟s where you … I think a drink was somewhere like 90 cents, it wasn‟t quite a dollar, I think, you know. Then the next section was just chairs only, where you didn‟t have to drink, you just—everybody had to pay admission—but if you sit there, you could sit all night, not spending any more money.
